14.  Regulation 40 of Listing Regulations, as amended, 
mandates that transfer, transmission and 
transposition of securities of listed companies held 
in physical form shall be effected only in demat 
mode. Further, SEBI, vide its Circular number  
SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD_RTAMB/P/CIR/2022/8 
dated January 25, 2022 and SEBI Circular 
HO/38/13/(3)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/3763/2026 dated  
January 30, 2026 has clarified that listed companies, with immediate effect, shall issue the securities 
only in demat mode while processing investor 
service requests pertaining to issuance of duplicate 
shares, exchange of shares, endorsement, sub-
division/ consolidation of share certificates, etc. 
In view of this as well as to eliminate all risks 
associated with physical shares and for ease of 
portfolio management, Members holding shares in 
physical form are requested to consider converting 
their holdings to demat mode.
15.  To prevent fraudulent transactions, Members 
are requested to exercise due diligence and 
immediately notify to the RTA any change in 
their address and/or bank mandate in respect of 
shares held in physical form and to their DPs in 
respect of shares held in the dematerialized form. 
Members are also advised not to leave their demat 
account(s) dormant for long. Periodic statement of 
holdings should be obtained from the concerned DP 
and holdings should be verified.
16.  The Securities and Exchange Board of India (‘SEBI’) 
has mandated the submission of Permanent Account 
Number (‘PAN’) by every participant in securities 
market. Members holding shares in electronic form 
are, therefore, requested to submit their PAN to their 
DPs with whom they are maintaining their demat 
accounts. Members holding shares in physical form 
can submit their PAN to the Company/ RTA.
17.  Pursuant to Section 72 of the Act, member(s) of 
the Company may nominate a person in whom the 
shares held by him/them shall vest in the event 
of his/ their unfortunate death. Member(s) holding 
shares in physical form may file nomination in 
the prescribed Form SH-13 with the Company’s 
Registrar and Transfer Agent (RTA). In respect of 
shares held in dematerialized form, the nomination 
form may be filed with the respective Depository 
Participant.

  How do I vote electronically using NSDL e-Voting system?
  The way to vote electronically on NSDL e-Voting system consists of “Two Steps” which are mentioned below:
 Step 1: Access to NSDL e-Voting system
A)  Login method for e-Voting and joining virtual meeting for Individual shareholders holding securities in 
demat mode
  In terms of SEBI Master Circular No. HO/49/14/14(7)2025-CFD-POD2/I/3762/2026 dated January 30, 2026 
individual shareholders holding securities in demat mode are allowed to vote through their demat account 
maintained with Depositories and Depository Participants. Shareholders are advised to update their mobile 
number and email Id in their demat accounts to access e-Voting facility.
 Login method for Individual shareholders holding securities in demat mode is given below:
Type of shareholders  Login Method
Individual Shareholders 
holding securities in 
demat mode with NSDL.1.  For OTP based login you can click on https://eservices.nsdl.com/SecureWeb/evoting/
evotinglogin.jsp . You will have to enter your 8-digit DP ID,8-digit Client Id, PAN No., 
Verification code and generate OTP. Enter the OTP received on registered email id/mobile 
number and click on login. After successful authentication, you will be redirected to NSDL 
Depository site wherein you can see e-Voting page. Click on company name or e-Voting 
service provider i.e. NSDL  and you will be redirected to e-Voting website of NSDL for 
casting your vote during the remote e-Voting period or joining virtual meeting & voting 
during the meeting.
2.  Existing IDeAS  user can visit the e-Services website of NSDL Viz. https://eservices.nsdl.
com either on a Personal Computer or on a mobile. On the e-Services home page click 
on the “Beneficial Owner”  icon under “Login”  which is available under ‘IDeAS’  
section, this will prompt you to enter your existing User ID and Password. After successful 
authentication, you will be able to see e-Voting services under Value added services. Click 
on “Access to e-Voting”  under e-Voting services and you will be able to see e-Voting 
page. Click on company name or e-Voting service provider i.e. NSDL  and you will be 
re-directed to e-Voting website of NSDL for casting your vote during the remote e-Voting 
period or joining virtual meeting & voting during the meeting.

Manner of holding shares i.e. Demat

 c) How to retrieve your ‘initial password’?

confirmation page.7.  Once you confirm your vote on the resolution, you

the premier hotel chains in India with a consistent track 
record of profitability and growth.

as a part of succession planning, Mr. Patanjali Govind

completion of his current tenure. In this role, his

the Company’s long-term vision, strategic direction,

=== page 16 ===
A Contemporary 
Platform for Indian 
Hospitality
Lemon Tree Hotels was built around a clear need gap in the market. 
In the early 2000s, nearly 80% of India’s branded hotel inventory was 
concentrated in the upper upscale, upscale and luxury segments, while 
the midscale and economy categories remained largely underserved. This 
created the opportunity to build a hospitality brand for travellers seeking 
quality, consistency and safety at accessible price points.
The Company opened its first hotel in May 2004, with 49 rooms. Today, 
Lemon Tree Hotels Limited has a portfolio of 268 hotels, including 131 
operational properties and 137 in the pipeline across India and international 
markets.
With a diversified portfolio of owned, leased, managed and franchised 
hotels spanning the upscale, upper midscale, midscale and economy 
segments, the Company is strategically positioned to cater to a broad 
spectrum of business and leisure travellers. Its strategy is to build a truly 
national hospitality network across India while selectively expanding its 
international footprint in high-potential markets. This enables the Company 
to serve a diverse customer base through a multi-brand, multi-segment 
approach, strengthen brand recognition and deliver sustainable  
long-term growth.
Keys Select by Lemon Tree Hotels, UdaipurLemon Tree Hotels Limited
Integrated Annual Report 2025-26
Growth. Leadership. Responsibility.The Evolution of Excellence
When Lemon Tree Hotels 
started operations in 2004 with 
a 49-room hotel, we were not 
only entering the hospitality 
business, we were responding 
to a clear need in the market. 
India’s branded hotel industry 
had room to become broad- 
based, economically accessible 
and more relevant to a new 
generation of travellers.
Over the past two decades, that 
belief has shaped our growth. 
We have built brands across 
segments, expanded through 
multiple operating models 
and created a platform that 
serves business and leisure 
travellers across India and select 
international markets. Each 
stage of our journey has made 
us more focused, more resilient 
and better prepared for the 
opportunities ahead.PRELUDE
FY 2025-26 marks an important 
moment in this evolution. Our 
operating strength and financial 
performance have given us the 
confidence to undertake the 
proposed Composite Scheme 
of Arrangement. This step is 
intended to create two distinct 
yet complementary businesses: 
an asset-heavy hotel ownership 
company and an asset-light 
management and franchising 
company, each with a clear 
strategic mandate and capital 
allocation framework.
For us, this is more than a 
change in structure. It is a way 
to give each company the clarity, 
capital discipline and strategic 
focus it needs to grow well over 
the next two decades and more.This is the thinking behind the 
theme of this year’s report.
Growth means expanding with 
intention, not simply scale.
Leadership means making 
anticipatory choices that prepare 
us for the future.
Responsibility means ensuring 
that our progress continues to 
create value for our people, 
guests, shareholders, partners 
and communities.
As we move forward, we do so 
with the same belief that shaped 
our beginning: hospitality grows 
stronger when it is relevant, 
accessible and responsibly built.

A Clear PurposeHospitality with 
Lemon Tree Hotels Limited is India’s largest hotel 
chain in the mid-market, spanning the upper-
midscale, midscale and economy segments and the 
third-largest overall by number of rooms. With a 
portfolio of brands designed for the needs of business 
and leisure travellers, we combine quality service, 
operating efficiency and value-led offerings to deliver 
a consistent guest experience across our network.
Core 
ValuesVision
Lemon Tree Hotels shall be the largest and most 
preferred Indian chain of upper-upscale, upscale, 
upper-midscale, midscale and economy hotels 
and resorts.
Mission
We shall be committed to:
• Ensuring the well-being and self-worth of our 
colleagues, who are of the utmost importance  
to us
• Contributing to the community we live in and to 
India in general
• Delighting our guests, whose comfort, safety, 
security and well-being are our main reason for 
being
• Rewarding our stakeholders, whose trust 
motivates us to excel further
• Protecting the environment
• Maximising the efficiency of our processes, to 
enable us to be the most cost-effective brand 
offering the greatest value, which our customers

Strategic ReorganisationUnlocking Value through   
During  FY 2025-26, our Board of Directors approved a Composite Scheme 
of Arrangement to reshape our corporate and hotel ownership structure. The 
proposed reorganisation is intended to create two clearly defined businesses, 
each with its own operating model, capital needs and path to growth.

16Lemon Tree Hotels Limited
Integrated Annual Report 2025-26
Under this scheme, Lemon Tree Hotels 
Limited will transition into a pure-play, 
high-margin, asset-light brand and 
management company. Concurrently, 
Fleur Hotels Limited (material subsidiary 
of the Company) will be established as 
a dedicated, large-scale hotel ownership 
and development company, backed by 
a primary capital infusion from Warburg 
Pincus and positioned for an independent 
public listing. By separating the two 
companies, we optimise capital allocation, 
sharpen operational focus and unlock 
clear, long-term intrinsic value for all 
stakeholders.Key Elements of the Proposed Restructuring
The proposed restructuring involves three steps:
• Warburg Pincus to acquire APG’s entire 41.09% stake in Fleur 
Hotels Limited. Subsequent to year ended 31 March 2026, on  
22 May 2026, Warburg has acquired APG’s entire stake of 
41.09% in Fleur Hotels Limited
• Lemon Tree Hotels Limited will transfer 17 hotels (15 operational 
and 2 under construction), along with its development 
capabilities, to Fleur Hotels Limited post 31 March 2026. In 
consideration, Fleur will issue new equity shares to Lemon Tree 
Hotels Limited and its shareholders
• Upon completion of the Scheme and the receipt of the 
necessary approvals, Fleur Hotels Limited is proposed to be 
listed as an independent company

India’s Hospitality 
Growth Story
India’s hospitality industry has 
entered a new phase of structural 
growth, driven by resilient 
domestic demand, expanding 
infrastructure and evolving 
travel preferences. The mid-
priced hotel segment is uniquely 
positioned at the sweet spot of 
this growth trajectory, benefiting 
from a rapidly expanding middle 
class, rising disposable incomes 
and an increasing preference 
for branded, standardized 
experiences across Tier I, 
II, III, IV cities. As value-
conscious corporate and leisure 
travellers actively seek quality 
accommodations at accessible 
price points, the mid-market 
segment is projected to 
outperform the broader industry 
in supply expansion, room 
demand and occupancy gains 
over the coming decade.
Demonstrating strong operational 
resilience and sustained pricing 
power, the market maintained 
healthy occupancy levels of  
63-65%, with Average Room 
Rates (ARRs) strengthening to 
₹ 8,500-₹ 8,700 and RevPAR 
growing by 10-12% year-on-
year5. These robust numbers 
reflect high consumer demand 
for hotels across segments, 
driven by rising affordability, 
faster corporate travel recovery and a structural shift toward 
branded stays over unorganized 
alternatives. The numbers point 
to significant, scalable growth 
potential going forward. At the 
same time, hotel development 
momentum remains strong with 
over 64,000 branded hotel keys 
signed across 586 properties, 
highlighting investor confidence 
in India’s long-term hospitality 
story5.
Travel demand is also becoming 
increasingly diverse. Destination 
weddings, religious/spiritual 
tourism, live performances 
and shows, MICE events and 
experiential leisure travel are 
emerging as significant demand

continues to expand beyond

our presence across high-
potential destinations, delivering 
memorable guest experiences 
and creating sustainable value 
as India’s hospitality landscape 
continues to evolve.
A Transformational Step 
towards the Future
FY 2025-26 was also one of 
the most defining years in 
our strategic evolution. We 
announced a Composite Scheme 
of Arrangement - the proposed 
reorganisation will result in 
two distinct, well-capitalised 
companies - Lemon Tree Hotels 
as a pure-play asset-light 
company focused on offering 
hotel management, brand and 
loyalty, distribution and digital 
services. Fleur Hotels as a large-
scale growth-oriented hotel 
ownership/leasing company 
with end-to-end in-house 
development capabilities and a 
potentially large pipeline with 
a significant pool of available 
capital. Each company will have 
its own management team, 
capital structure, governance 
and growth priorities, while 
continuing to benefit from long-
term operating arrangements and strategic alignment. We view 
this not as a culmination, but as 
the beginning of the next chapter 
in Lemon Tree’s journey.
Over the past decade, we 
have built a unique hospitality 
ecosystem spanning ownership, 
development, management and 
franchising. As the business 
has scaled, it has become clear 
that these companies have 
different capital requirements 
and growth trajectories. Allowing 
each to follow its own strategic 
roadmap, while continuing to 
draw on the strength of the 
Lemon Tree brand, is the natural 
next step in our evolution. This 
is also completely in line with 
how mature hospitality markets 
have developed globally. The 
structure has been designed to 
ensure our shareholders continue 
to participate in the growth and 
value creation of both companies. 
The scheme has already achieved 
important regulatory milestones 
and we remain committed to 
executing it with the same 
discipline and transparency that 
has guided Lemon Tree’s journey 
since inception.
This demerger will enhance 
operational focus, improve 
capital efficiency and enable each 
business to pursue its growth 
ambitions independently while 
unlocking greater long-term 
value. Importantly, our existing 
shareholders will continue to 
participate directly in the future 
growth and value creation of 
both companies. A significant 
milestone in this journey has 
been the induction of Warburg 
Pincus as a strategic investor 
and long-term capital partner 
for Fleur Hotels, reinforcing 
confidence in the strength of 
our vision and the quality of our 
asset company.

Delivering Another Year 
of Growth
Our strategic momentum was 
matched by another record 
year of operational and financial 
growth. From a leadership 
perspective, we evaluate our 
performance not merely by 
top-line expansion, but by 
the quality, predictability and 
sustainability of our cash flows. 
Total revenue grew 13% year-
on-year to ₹ 1,452.7 Crores, 
driven by structural operating 
leverage as our mature inventory 
operated at a record 73.5%6 
occupancy with Gross ARR of 
₹ 6,8756. Net EBITDA rose 10% 
to ₹ 699.3 Crores, Profit After 
Tax expanded 19% to ₹ 288.3 
Crores and Cash Profit grew 16% 
to ₹ 443.1 Crores. Crucially, 
we converted this operational 
cash flow into balance sheet 
resilience, deleveraging total 
debt to ₹ 1,500 Crores while 
reducing our weighted average 
cost of debt by 115 basis points 
to 7.42%. Meanwhile, our 
transition toward a capital-light 
model gathered momentum as 
we operationalised 20 managed 
and franchised properties and 
signed 56 new hotel contracts, 
expanding our total hotel 
inventory to 268 hotels and 
22,581 rooms across more 
than 160 cities, driving a 14% 
increase in management fee 
income to ₹ 169.7 Crores.
In FY26, our margins were 
impacted by 580 basis points 
due to a significant step-up in 
renovation expenditure as we 
invest in upgrading our owned 
hotel portfolio, investments in 
technology and the GST-related 
change that came into effect 
during the year, which only had 
a half-year impact in FY26 and 
will have a full-year impact going 
forward. This GST impact will 
decrease year-on-year as the 
numbers of customers paying 
a rate below ₹ 7,500 keeps 
reducing in the medium term, 
with our price hikes/ARR growth. 
Additionally, nearly all our hotel 
ownership future supply is being planned under the upscale Aurika 
brand which remains largely 
unaffected by this change. We 
expect all these 3 expense 
heads to reduce to ~3.7% of 
revenue by FY 2027-28 and 
beyond, leading to corresponding 
expansion in EBITDA margins.

Travel LandscapeAn Evolving 
India’s travel and tourism sector continued to expand 
during the year, supported by rising domestic travel, 
improving connectivity and wider digital adoption. 
Demand grew across leisure, business, events and 
extended-stay travel, while emerging destinations and 
new travel formats broadened the market further. 
Traveller expectations also continued to change. 
Convenience, consistency, value, ﬂexibility and 
personalised experiences increasingly shaped decisions 
around where to travel, how to book and which 
hospitality brands to choose. These trends are creating a 
more diverse and segmented market, with opportunities 
across locations, formats and price points.OPERATING ENVIRONMENT
Lemon Tree Hotel, SonmargLemon Tree Hotels Limited
Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 36
India’s hospitality sector continues to benefit from 
long-term growth in domestic travel, infrastructure 
development and consumer spending. Domestic Tourist 
Visits reached approximately 4.55 billion in 202511, 
while total air passenger traffic exceeded 420 million11, 
indicating the growing scale of the country’s travel 
economy. Continued investment in airports, highways 
and tourism infrastructure is improving access and 
supporting hospitality demand across both established 
and emerging business and leisure destinations.
India’s hospitality market is expanding beyond its 
traditional gateway cities. Better connectivity, more 
dispersed economic activity and rising local demand 
are supporting hotel development across Tier II, 
Tier III and emerging urban centres. More than 
64,000 hotel keys were signed in 202511, with a 
significant share located in these markets, reflecting 
growing developer and investor interest.
Our Response
Our expansion strategy places a clear emphasis on non-metro markets. Managed and franchised hotels now 
account for more than 6,000 keys, representing over half of our portfolio of 11,800+ operating rooms. During 
FY 2025-26, we signed 56 hotels comprising 4,959 keys, with much of this pipeline located in underpenetrated 
regional markets. Our multi-brand portfolio, including Aurika Hotels & Resorts, Lemon Tree Premier, Lemon 
Tree Hotels, Red Fox by Lemon Tree Hotels, Keys Prima by Lemon Tree Hotels, Keys Select by Lemon Tree 
Hotels and Keys Lite by Lemon Tree Hotels, allows us to match each hotel to the demand profile of its location. 
This gives us the flexibility to enter new markets with the right product and build our presence as travel 
demand develops.Capitalising on India’s Structural 
T ourism Growth 
Expansion Beyond 
Metro CitiesOur Response
During FY 2025-26, we announced a strategic demerger to create two focused businesses with distinct 
purposes. Lemon Tree Hotels is transitioning into a debt-free, asset-light brand management and loyalty 
platform, targeting a steady-state EBITDA margin of 70%+. Fleur Hotels, backed by Warburg Pincus, will 
operate as a separate asset ownership and development platform. The structure is designed to support faster 
portfolio growth while limiting the need for additional capital on Lemon Tree Hotels’ balance sheet. It will also 
allow us to convert a larger share of our growth into recurring, fee-based revenue.

Faith-based tourism has become an important 
driver of domestic travel in India. The Maha 
Kumbh drew more than 663 million visitors12, 
demonstrating the scale of travel associated 
with major spiritual events. At the same 
time, growing interest in heritage, wildlife and 
cultural experiences is broadening demand 
across destinations and thereby creating new 
opportunities for hospitality operators going 
beyond traditional business and leisure markets.
Travellers are placing greater value on the 
quality of the stay, not only the destination itself. 
Personalised service, wellness, local cuisine and 
experiences rooted in the character of a place are 
becoming more important in travel decisions. This 
is influencing how hotels design their offerings, 
while supporting longer stays and greater 
willingness to spend on distinctive experiences.
Our Response
We are expanding our presence across key religious and cultural destinations, including Rishikesh, Haridwar, Katra, 
Mukteshwar, Somnath, Tirupati and Dwarka which are renowned for their spiritual significance, as well as Agra, 
Aurangabad, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Jaipur, Udaipur, Kumbhalgarh, Jhansi and Lucknow that are celebrated for their 
rich heritage. Through our managed portfolio, we bring hotels with consistently high standards of hygiene, service 
and comfort to markets that have traditionally been more fragmented. These destinations attract steady demand 
from families and multi-generational travellers, often across different times of the year. By aligning our brands 
and hotel formats with local market needs, we are building a more balanced portfolio across business, leisure and 
pilgrimage travel.
Our Response
We have created Aurika Hotels & Resorts, our upscale brand, through properties such as Aurika, Udaipur and 
Aurika, Mumbai Skycity. Each hotel is designed to offer a distinct sense of local design, supported by destination-
led dining, wellness and curated guest experiences. The growth of this portfolio has strengthened our presence in 
the premium leisure and urban hospitality segments. It also supported an increase in our group’s Average Room 
Rate to ₹ 6,875 in FY 2025-26, while contributing to higher total revenue per available room.Religious and Cultural T ourism

performance.

We are integrating sustainability more deeply into the way we operate our hotels through a focused set 
of environmental initiatives. These include increasing the use of renewable energy through rooftop solar 
installations, open access agreements and green power purchases. In FY 2025-26, renewable energy accounted 
for 39.38% of our annual electricity consumption, with an exit rate of 50.66%.
We continue to strengthen water stewardship by expanding water treatment and recycling systems across our 
properties. As a result, we reduced water intensity (KL/m³) by 9.77% in FY 2025-26 compared with the  
FY 2018-19 baseline. We are also enhancing energy efficiency through the adoption of high-performance HVAC 
systems and other energy-efficient building technologies.
As part of our commitment to sustainable infrastructure, all 41 of our owned and leased hotels have been 
certified as green buildings by the Indian Green Building Council (IGBC).
These initiatives have enabled us to significantly reduce our environmental footprint, with GHG emissions 
intensity (tCO₂e/m³) declining by 35.74% in FY 2025-26 compared with the FY 2018-19 baseline. Beyond their 
environmental impact, these efforts help optimise resource consumption, improve operating efficiency and 
manage costs, while strengthening our appeal to environmentally conscious guests and meeting the evolving 
sustainability expectations of corporate and institutional customers.Increasing Focus on 
Sustainability

Material PrioritiesDeﬁning our  
Aligned with GRI and SASB guidelines, we conducted a materiality assessment in 
FY 2020-21 to determine the issues most material to our business and stakeholders. 
Adopting a quadripartite approach, we identified and prioritised key economic and 
ESG themes that guide our strategic decision-making and sustainability disclosures.MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT
Our Approach to Materiality Assessment
1. Identification  
 Compiled a comprehensive list of material topics 
by integrating GRI and SASB guidelines with peer 
benchmarking insights.
2. Categorisation  
 Classified each topic under the Environmental, 
Social and Governance (ESG) pillars to identify 
themes most relevant to LTH.
3. Prioritisation  
 Developed a materiality matrix and stakeholder 
priority map based on stakeholder consultations to 
rank key material topics.
4. Validation  
 Validated the materiality assessment through 
collaboration with management and an external 
assurance agency to ensure a comprehensive and 
unbiased evaluation of material issues.

Energy Efficiency
Across our portfolio, LED lighting continues to reduce energy consumption compared to conventional fixtures. In 
installed areas, it cuts lighting load energy use by up to 80%. Variable frequency drives on relevant equipment 
reduce energy consumption by 10-20%. They also improve process control while lowering electricity costs. Heat 
pumps across select properties continue to reduce utility costs and carbon emissions. Their low payback period 
supports broader deployment.
As part of our ongoing renovation and 
upgrade program across 41 owned/
leased hotels, we have redefined our 
electrical design model and expanded 
the use of electrically powered 
equipment. The number of heat 
pumps increased ninefold, from 3 in 
FY 2018-19 to 27 in FY 2025-26, while 
EV charging stations increased from 
none to 22. We also commissioned  
19 water-bottling plants for safe 
drinking water, replacing single-use 
plastic bottles, compared with none in  
FY 2018-19.Energy-Efficiency Measures Undertaken in FY 2025-26
Heat Pumps
Heat pumps installed across 
17 owned hotels and 1 
managed hotel in Ahmedabad, 
Bengaluru, Chennai, Kochi, 
Delhi, Gurugram, Kaushambi, 
Hyderabad, Indore, Noida 
and Pune. The pumps provide 
hot water for guest rooms, 
kitchens and laundries. By 
delivering three to four units 
of heat for every unit of 
electricity consumed, they can 
reduce the energy required 
for water heating by 50-70%. 
They also lower dependence 
on diesel- and gas-fired 
boilers, helping reduce 
operating costs and carbon 
emissions. Variable Frequency 
Drives for Chillers
Variable Frequency Drives 
installed at 2 hotels, in 
Indore and Kaushambi, 
adjust compressor and 
motor speeds according 
to the actual cooling load, 
instead of allowing the 
equipment to operate 
continuously at full speed. 
This can reduce HVAC 
energy consumption by 
10-20%, while lowering 
equipment wear and tear, 
reducing maintenance 
requirements and 
improving guest comfort. Air Handling Units 
for HV AC Systems 
Efficient Air Handling 
Units across 5 hotels 
in Dehradun, Jaipur, 
Kaushambi, Ludhiana 
and Indore. They filter, 
cool and circulate air 
in public areas while 
regulating humidity. 
Their efficient operation 
helps maintain indoor 
comfort and air quality 
while reducing energy 
consumption. Solar Reflectance 
Index Paint on 
Terraces
Applied across 10 
hotels in Bengaluru, 
Chandigarh, Kochi, 
Dehradun, Gurugram, 
Hyderabad, Udaipur and 
Vishakhapatnam, this 
high-reflectance cool-
roof coating reduces the 
amount of heat absorbed 
through hotel terraces. 
This helps lower the 
air-conditioning load 
on upper floors while 
supporting a longer  
roof life.
Energy requirements also increased 
due to higher cooling needs amid 
rising ambient temperatures, 
enhanced in-house laundry capacity 
and the transition of kitchen and 
buffet operations from gas- and 
coal-fired equipment to electric 
alternatives, including induction 
appliances. Product upgrades added 
equipment such as dishwashers, 
under-counter units and motors 
across the portfolio. In addition, 
while the total floor area remained 
unchanged year-on-year, the portfolio recorded an average of 
111 additional rooms sold per 
day in FY 2025-26 compared 
with FY 2024-25. The Aurika 
portfolio, comprising 808 rooms 
and representing 14% of the total 
owned inventory, also has a higher 
Energy Performance Index than 
the other Lemon Tree brands. 
Collectively, these operational and 
portfolio changes contributed to 
higher energy consumption across 
the 41 owned/leased hotels.Change in Energy Intensity: FY 2025-26

Renewable Energy (RE)
By the end of FY 2025-26, we 
achieved a renewable energy exit 
rate of 50.66%, in line with our 
target. Our RE mix includes solar 
photovoltaic systems installed 
across our properties, open-
access RE agreements for hotels 
in Delhi, Bengaluru, Mumbai, Pune 
and Chennai and Green Power 
Purchase agreements with the 
respective State Electricity Boards 
in Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Mumbai 
and Pune.
During FY 2025-26, rooftop solar 
photovoltaic systems were installed across 7 owned hotels in Bengaluru, 
Delhi, Gurugram and Hyderabad to 
generate renewable electricity on-
site. These installations help reduce 
dependence on grid electricity, 
lower energy costs, mitigate 
exposure to rising tariffs and 
reduce carbon emissions.
We continue to assess captive and 
group-captive RE opportunities 
in select states. Implementation 
will be considered following the 
completion of due diligence and 
financial feasibility assessments.Our RE strategy combines on-site 
and offsite sources. On-site RE 
improves energy independence 
and reduces reliance on fossil 
fuels, lowering costs and our 
carbon footprint at the properties 
where it is installed. Meanwhile, 
offsite RE expands access to clean 
power beyond on-site generation, 
reducing grid dependency while 
supporting RE development and 
grid resilience. Together, these 
approaches support our progress 
toward a fully renewable energy 
portfolio.

We measure and monitor our 
Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions 
from energy consumption across 
our hotels. We have identified 
several measures to reduce our 
carbon footprint. These include 
increasing our use of renewable 
energy, deploying energy-efficient 
equipment and shifting to cleaner 
fuels such as LPG and CNG instead 
of higher-emission alternatives. We 
are also implementing an action plan to introduce EVs across our 
hotels and exploring carbon offsets 
to address emissions we cannot yet 
eliminate.
To further reduce emissions, 
we are replacing equipment 
that uses chlorofluorocarbons. 
We are also upgrading older air 
conditioning systems with units 
that use low Global Warming 
Potential and Ozone Depletion 
Potential refrigerants, such as R32 and R410. In addition, our diesel 
generators are equipped with Retro 
Emission Control Devices that 
capture more than 90% of carbon 
particulate matter from exhaust, 
improving air quality. Dual Fuel Kits 
also enable generators to operate 
on a blend of diesel and gaseous 
fuel, reducing both emissions and 
operating costs.

Water Stewardship
We build water efficiency into our guest-facing infrastructure. Dual-flush systems reduce water use by up to 60% 
per flush compared to conventional fixtures. Water-efficient fixtures across our properties can also be customized 
to reduce water use and lower water bills without affecting the guest experience. Together, these measures help 
reduce pressure on local water resources wherever they are installed.

Ozonation system for 
swimming pools
An ozonation system was installed 
at one owned hotel in Hyderabad. 
The system disinfects pool water 
using ozone, reducing chlorine 
consumption, chemical costs and 
water wastage, while providing 
clearer water with less odour and

STP/ETP systems
Sewage and Effluent Treatment 
Plants were implemented 
at four owned hotels across

systems treat wastewater for safe

Ultrafiltration system
An ultrafiltration system was 
installed at one owned hotel in Delhi to further treat water 
processed through the Sewage 
Treatment Plant. Fine membranes 
remove suspended solids, bacteria 
and turbidity, producing clear water 
for reuse in flushing, gardening 
and cooling towers. The system 
improves water recovery, reduces 
wastewater discharge and protects 
downstream reverse osmosis and 
boiler equipment from fouling.
Water-bottling RO plants and 
reusable glass bottles
As a part of our strategy to ‘Say No 
To Plastic’, during FY 2025-26, 
10 hotels across Alleppey 
(Kerala), Bengaluru, Hyderabad, 
Jaipur, Kochi, Kolkata, Pune and 
Thiruvananthapuram installed 
water-bottling RO plants. These 
were in addition to 9 existing 
plants across Bengaluru, Delhi, 
Gurugram, Mumbai and Udaipur, 
taking the total number of hotels 
to 19. The plants purify and bottle 
drinking water on-site in reusable glass bottles, replacing single-
use packaged plastic water and 
reducing recurring procurement and 
transportation requirements. The 
process follows prescribed cleaning, 
sanitising, filling, packaging and 
date-stamped labelling protocols to 
maintain water quality and safety. 
Across all bottling plants, plastic 
savings increased from 19,548 kg  
in FY 2024-25 to 39,277 kg in  
FY 2025-26.
Capacitive De-ionization 
technology
We also use Capacitive  
De-ionization technology for 
water purification and softening, 
for example, at Aurika, Mumbai 
Skycity. The system can recover 
up to 90% of the water processed, 
reduce total dissolved solids by up 
to 90% and consume approximately 
30% of the electricity required 
by conventional Reverse Osmosis 
systems.

CASE STUDY
Replacing Plastic Key Cards with Wooden Alternatives
During FY 2025-26, we replaced plastic key cards with wooden alternatives to reduce plastic use in 
guest-facing operations.
The initiative covered 28 hotels and 25,200 key cards, resulting in a saving of 151.20 kg of plastic 
across the portfolio. It also reduced key card costs by 22.22% compared with plastic cards.

CASE STUDY
Repurposing Used Guest Soap through Soap For Hope™
Soap For Hope™ repurposes partially used guest soap collected from hotels into new soap bars for 
distribution to communities where they are needed.
In FY 2025-26, the initiative covered 40 owned/leased, managed/franchised hotels across 12 cities: 
Delhi, Gurugram, Noida, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Chennai, Goa, Jaipur, Indore, Jhansi and 
Alleppey (Kerala). During the year, we repurposed 2,186 kg of used guest soap for community 
distribution.

Employee Engagement
Talent matters to us regardless of 
gender, background or individual 
need and that principle shapes 
how we hire and develop our 
people. We also keep our hierarchy 
intentionally lean, creating more 
opportunities for collaboration and 
participation across teams instead 
of slowing ideas through multiple 
layers. Bringing young talent into 
the organisation at every level 
reflects the same approach, as 
fresh perspectives support our 
long-term growth.
We apply the same openness to 
how we engage with employees 
every day. Hotel level town halls 
and team-building activities 
keep communication open and 
strengthen collaboration across 
teams. "Fresh-eyes" discussions 
give new joiners a dedicated 
forum to share their early 
impressions, while weekly one-
on-one conversations between 
hotel managers and employees 
help us address individual needs 
as they arise. Depending on the 
forum, these conversations take 
place weekly, monthly, quarterly or 
annually, covering health, safety, 
well-being, talent management, 
diversity and inclusion, ethics and 
transparency.

Diversity and Inclusion
Our Diversity and Inclusion Policy is built on trust, responsibility and long-term socio-economic development for our 
people and the communities around our hotels. For nearly two decades, we have upheld equal opportunity in hiring. 
It continues to guide how we hire, promote and support our people.
As part of this commitment, we focus on Opportunity Deprived Individuals (ODIs), including Employees with 
Disability (EwD) and people from Economically and Socially marginalised backgrounds (EcoSoc). By welcoming 
ODIs into our teams, we provide access to stable, dignified employment while making our guest experience more 
inclusive.

Our commitment to hiring 
Opportunity Deprived Individuals 
began in 2007 with EWDs and 
expanded in 2016 to include 
EcoSocs. Nearly two decades later, 
we support people across a broad 
range of disability types, including 
speech and hearing impairment, 
orthopedic disability, low vision, 
acid survivors and intellectual and 
developmental disabilities such 
as Down Syndrome, autism and 
slow learners. Employees with 
speech and hearing impairment 
remain our largest group. We 
also hire individuals below the 
poverty line, widowed or destitute 
women, orphans and abandoned 
girls, transgender persons, school 
dropouts and people from regions 
with limited access to education 
and employment.
Our commitment to inclusion 
extends beyond just hiring to 
how we train and support our 
people. Every employee learns 
Indian Sign Language (ISL) and is 
assessed on it. Training is tailored 
to different needs. Deaf colleagues 
attend integrated sessions led by 
a trainer and an ISL interpreter. 
Low vision colleagues receive 
accessible learning materials. 
Colleagues with intellectual and 
developmental disability or autism complete internships of more than 
six months instead of classroom 
training. Supervisors and managers 
also receive training to help 
new team members during this 
transition. Today, this approach is Key Diversity and Inclusion Initiatives
followed across our hotels and we 
continue sharing our experience 
with organisations in hospitality and 
other sectors in India and abroad.
CASE STUDY
Continuing its focus on 
inclusive hiring, LTH created 
internship opportunities for 
neurodivergent individuals, 
including those with intellectual 
and developmental disabilities 
(IDD) and autism.

Bengaluru, Bhopal, Chennai, 
Delhi and Gurugram in 
partnership with Mann NGO,

Solutions, Diya Foundation

joined the LTH team through 
employment or apprenticeship 
opportunities, while 6 will 
continue their internships into 
FY 2026-27. A few interns chose to return to their

training.
LTH is also exploring

for autistic youth in Mumbai 
and young adults with specific

Learning and Development
We view learning and development as central to building capable teams, strengthening operational consistency 
and delivering memorable guest experiences. Our programs support employees through structured onboarding, 
functional capability building and continuous improvement.
Functional Champion Program
The Functional Champion Program is a structured 
onboarding initiative designed to support the seamless 
integration of newly appointed hotel-level Heads 
of Department. Upon joining, each new Head of 
Department is assigned a Functional Champion, who 
serves as a buddy, mentor and guide throughout the 
first two months. The program provides continuous 
support and helps new leaders understand their roles, 
responsibilities and operational expectations. Its 
completion is an important milestone in the employee 
confirmation process, ensuring alignment with Lemon 
Tree Hotels’ operational standards.
Protel PMS (Part of Front Office 101)
The arrival and departure experience is a critical driver 
of guest satisfaction. To support a seamless guest 
journey, Learning and Development trainers must have 
a thorough understanding of the Property Management 
System used across hotel operations. The Protel PMS is 
a part of Front Office 101 and it equips team members 
to efficiently manage reservations, check-ins,  
check-outs, guest requests, billing and other key 
operational processes.
Quality Audits
To enhance the guest experience and strengthen 
operational excellence across Lemon Tree Hotels, 
we have developed a comprehensive Quality Audit 
Program. The initiative assesses hotel performance 
against defined brand standards and identifies 
opportunities for continuous improvement. The 
audit framework evaluates the four core operational 
departments, critical Moments of Truth across the 
guest journey, key guest touchpoints, brand essentials, 
hotel upkeep and innovation. It also reviews the culture 
of inclusion and the warm, friendly service that defines 
the Lemon Tree experience.

SHAs HiPots Overall EmployeesFY24 FY25 FY2646Launched in August 2024, our Hotel General Managers (HGMs) Development Program is an annual phenomenon. 
It is a structured three-month initiative which strengthens functional knowledge and builds leadership skills. HGMs 
go through online and in-person sessions led by Corporate Function Heads. Self-study, videos, simulations and live 
case work reinforce learning. The primary objective of this initiative is to develop well-rounded HGMs who embody 
Lemon Tree’s culture and DNA.
We opened 20 new hotels across India and overseas this past year. This expansion created growth opportunities 
for existing employees. Several advanced to Deputy Head of Department or Head of Department roles at new 
properties. Promoting from within also helps carry our culture into every new hotel.

Health, Safety and Well-Being
Every hotel operates under our Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Management System covering all 
employees. Routine and non-routine hazard identification is integrated into our operations. We work to achieve zero 
occupational health incidents across employees, contractors, guests, communities and the public.
Automatic smoke detectors, 
audible alarms, fire 
extinguishers, hydrants, 
portable firefighting 
equipment and emergency 
lighting are installed across 
all hotels
High-touch surfaces, 
including doorknobs, 
countertops, room keys and 
EDC machines, are cleaned 
and sanitised routinely
Health camps, smoking

Hazard Identification and Mitigation
Our Incident Tracking System helps identify 
potential hazards before they escalate. When an 
incident is reported, we act promptly and implement 
measures to prevent recurrence. We support this 
process with structured training, documented 
emergency response plans and regular safety audits. 
These audits encourage employees to identify and 
address risks as part of our ongoing safety efforts.Zero

Health and Safety Governance
Our OHS Committee sets corporate health and safety 
standards, rules and procedures. At each hotel, the 
local OHS Committee oversees regional compliance, 
analyzes incidents and prioritises corrective actions. 
Every hotel also maintains trained first-aid staff on-site 
to respond immediately to medical emergencies.
In FY 2025-26, health and safety training reached 
47.23% of our full-time employees across 41 owned/
leased hotels and 31 managed hotels. Training 
completion was 27.59% among male employees and 
45.25% among female employees.
Human Rights
Our Human Rights Policy sets clear expectations 
for employees, business partners and third-party 
contractors, aligned with the Universal Declaration of 
Human Rights (UDHR) and the International Labour 
Organization (ILO) Declaration. It supports our zero-
tolerance approach to sexual harassment, discrimination, 
child Labour, forced Labour and exploitation in any 
form. We also monitor construction sites for violations, 
misconduct and unfair treatment. We refer all reported 
violations to our Vigilance Officer for a full investigation.Employee Training on Health and Safety in FY26 (%)

Responsible Supply Chain Practices
Every vendor, supplier and service provider we work with follows our Supplier Code of Conduct. 
The Code aligns with international frameworks, including the Universal Declaration of Human 
Rights (UDHR) and International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions. It defines requirements 
for minimum wages, human rights, health and safety, environmental compliance, labour 
practices, freedom of association, ethical conduct and transparent operations.

Our Code defines the standards we expect suppliers to 
meet. We also encourage them to establish ESG goals 
that align with these expectations.
• Ethics and Governance:
  Legal compliance, conflict of interest prevention,

• Human Rights:
  Prohibition of child labour and human trafficking, 
fair wages, reasonable working hours and non-
discrimination
• Environmental Sustainability:
  Obtaining and maintaining all required 
environmental permits and licenses under

• Occupational Health and Safety:

commitment to sustainability and inclusive community

Governance Structure
We aim to create long-term value for all our 
stakeholders, including shareholders, employees, 
guests, business partners and society. To support this 
goal, our governance system instils transparency and 
efficiency across our corporate processes.Board Performance Evaluation
Each year, the Nomination and Remuneration 
Committee conducts a formal evaluation of our Board, 
its committees and individual Directors. The process 
aligns with the Companies Act, 2013 and applicable 
SEBI (LODR) Regulations. It begins with input from 
every Director and evaluates that input against 
predefined qualitative and quantitative parameters. 
These cover the Board’s role in strategy, performance 
monitoring, risk oversight, statutory and regulatory 
compliance, organizational culture and talent 
management.
Independent Directors separately evaluate the Non-
Independent Directors, including the Chairperson, 
as required by law. They also assess the Board’s 
overall effectiveness. Both evaluations follow a Board-
approved framework, ensuring a transparent, objective 
and balanced assessment of individual Directors, 
committees and the Board.Audit Committee

Code of Conduct and Policy Framework
Our Code of Conduct applies to every Board Member, the 
leadership team, senior management and employees. It 
reflects our commitment to fairness, transparency and 
professionalism, setting clear expectations for conduct 
across the organisation. We review and approve all 
related-party transactions, including those involving 
interested Directors or potential conflicts of interest, 
through the Audit Committee and the Board. Material 
transactions require specific Board approval. By following

Commitment to Compliance
The Board, senior management and Key Managerial 
Personnel (KMP) maintain strict compliance with 
applicable laws, regulations and notifications. We 
regularly review our compliance framework with the 
leadership team to keep it current. Directors and KMPs 
participate in structured briefings on SEBI (LODR) 
Regulations, CSR, ESG, stock exchange compliance 
requirements, policy updates and the Vigil Mechanism 
Policy. These sessions keep them aligned with evolving 
governance expectations. During FY 2025-26, there 
were no fines, penalties or non-monetary sanctions in 
relation to Stock Exchanges, SEBI or capital market 
regulations.
Internal Audit and Assurance
Alignment with Corporate Heads of 
Department (HoD)
•  Individual meetings with Corporate HoDs are 
held before each audit cycle begins, evaluating 
existing audit parameters and key focus areas and 
communicating any changes in SOPs or guidelines
•  Audit parameters are rated and the scope of 
execution is agreed before the audit process starts
•  Action plans agreed with each HoD are 
documented and shared through minutes of 
meetings with stakeholders including Corporate 
HoDs
•  A summary of key issues is presented to the Audit 
CommitteeAudit Execution and Field Closure
•  The respective hotel Cluster Head and General 
Manager (GM) are notified ahead of each audit
•  Surprise audits are done without advance notice to 
the hotel team itself
•  Audit queries are shared with process owners and 
exceptions are reported to both process owners 
and the hotel GM for discussion
•  A closure meeting with the hotel GM and respective 
HoDs takes place at the end of each audit
•  Post-discussion observations and audit ratings are 
agreed and signed off by the GM
Issues Compilation and Presentation to 
Stakeholders
•  Once all audits close, issues observed across hotels 
are compiled at the corporate level with ratings
•  Issues are shared department-wise with Corporate 
HoDs for reference and comment
•  A review meeting with Corporate HoDs is 
scheduled to discuss the issues raised
•  Discussions focus on root cause analysis and 
corresponding action plans
•  Action plans agreed with each HoD are 
documented and shared through minutes of 
meetings with relevant stakeholders including 
Corporate HoDs
•  A summary of key issues is presented to the Audit 
Committee

=== page 68 ===
We follow a structured grievance redressal framework 
to address concerns from employees, shareholders 
and other stakeholders. It promotes transparency, 
accountability and timely resolution. The Audit 
Committee oversees the framework, while its 
Chairperson handles exceptional matters.
Our Whistleblower Policy (Vigil Mechanism) supports 
this framework and complies with the Companies 
Act, 2013 and the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015. 
It provides secure channels to report unethical 
conduct, fraud, financial irregularities or Code of 
Conduct violations. The policy ensures confidentiality, 
protects whistleblowers from victimization and allows 
anonymous reporting through sealed letters or email 
to the Vigilance Officer (svp_hr@lemontreehotels.
com) or the Audit Committee Chairperson 
(praveengargias@gmail.com). Exceptional cases may be escalated directly to the Chairperson. All 
disclosures are investigated objectively, resolved within 
defined timelines and records are retained for at least 
five years.
General grievances are addressed through a structured 
escalation process where matters are resolved within 
24 to 72 hours. We reinforce awareness of the available 
reporting channels through the General Service 
Rules and Regulations and New Hire Orientation. 
Employees with grievances can write in to OurVoice@
lemontreehotels.com. We also review employee 
satisfaction data to identify recurring concerns and 
strengthen our processes. The framework further 
covers shareholder complaints relating to share 
transfers, allotments, refunds, certificates, financial 
statements and annual reports. During FY 2025-26, no 
grievances were left unresolved.Grievance Redressal and Whistleblower Mechanism

Data Privacy and Security
We prioritise data security and governance through a 
robust framework with defined cybersecurity measures. 
These measures protect stakeholder personal 
information. We regularly review and update our 
security protocols to address technological changes and 
evolving regulatory requirements. This helps prevent 
data loss, misuse, unauthorized disclosure, alteration 
and destruction.
Under our Data Privacy Policy, we clearly explain 
what personal data we collect, why we collect it and 
how we use, process, share and transfer it. We retain 
personal data only as long as necessary to meet legal, 
regulatory, contractual or statutory requirements. After 
that, we securely delete or archive the data.
To strengthen oversight, we engage internal auditors 
and, when needed, external auditors to conduct 
IT control audits every six months. We report any 
anomalies to the Board. No data breaches were 
recorded during FY 2025-26.Memberships and Industry Associations

demand grew ~5% year-on-year, demonstrating the structural resilience of India’s tourism appeal.

geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, aviation 
disruptions, an unseasonal monsoon and currency

India’s hotel sector delivered another year of healthy performance in CY2025, led by pricing discipline and sustained 
demand depth across both business and leisure segments.Note: FTAs for 2025 and 2026 represent anomaly years driven by geopolitical disruptions in key source markets, including Bangladesh and the

Quarterly Performance Trends (FY 2025-26)
Q1 FY 2025-26 (April–June 2025):  The 
year opened strongly, with ARR growing 12.4% 
year- on- year and occupancy broadly stable. Mumbai 
led performance with occupancy around 75% and 
average rates around ₹ 12,000. The top five markets 
by RevPAR for the quarter were Mumbai, New Delhi, 
Bengaluru, Chennai and Hyderabad. The NIFTY 
Tourism Index improved 8% during the quarter.
Q2 FY 2025-26 (July–September 2025):  
The sector moderated, as expected in the monsoon 
quarter, compounded by Indo-Pakistan geopolitical 
tensions and the Air India crash, which weighed on 
travel sentiment. Nationwide RevPAR still grew 6% 
year-on-year, evidencing pricing resilience. The top 
five markets by RevPAR for this quarter were Mumbai, 
New Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai and Hyderabad. The 
NIFTY Tourism Index declined 5.1% during the quarter.
Q3 FY 2025-26 (October–December 2025):  
The strongest quarter of the year. Nationwide 
RevPAR grew 44.7% quarter-on-quarter and 12.1% year- on- year, driven by festive demand, peak wedding 
season and strong inbound foreign tourism. The top 
five markets by RevPAR were Udaipur, New Delhi, 
Mumbai, Goa and Jaipur. The NIFTY Tourism Index 
declined 2.9% during the quarter even as sector 
fundamentals remained strong.
Q4 FY 2025-26 (January–March 2026):  In this 
quarter, leisure demand slowed, but corporate and 
MICE demand strengthened, with February being one 
of the strongest months. However, the Middle East 
crisis weighed on travel sentiment. Despite this, stable 
domestic demand and limited new supply supported 
ARR and RevPAR growth resulting in a 5% growth in 
ARR and a degrowth of 75 basis points in occupancy. 
Hence, the nationwide RevPAR grew 4.8% year-on-
year. The top five markets by RevPAR for this quarter 
were Udaipur, New Delhi, Mumbai, Goa and Jaipur. 
The NIFTY Tourism Index declined 24.4% during the 
quarter.

Hotel development activity reached record levels in CY2025. Brand signings totalled 64,118 keys across 586

long-term hospitality fundamentals.
Management agreements remained the dominant growth model, accounting for over 85% of all keys signed 
in CY2025. Greenfield projects represented 59.5% of signings by keys, while conversions contributed 10.1%, 
evidencing the growing role of soft-brand strategies in capturing India’s vast independent hotel inventory.Q1

4. Key Demand Drivers
Business Travel
Corporate travel remains anchored in Delhi NCR, 
Mumbai, Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad. Record 
Grade-A office absorption — with weighted rentals 
reaching ₹ 101 per sq. ft. per month in Q3 FY 2025- 26 
and vacancy rates declining to 14.6% — signals 
continued expansion of the corporate workforce and, 
by extension, sustained business travel demand.
Leisure Travel
Leisure demand is the fastest-growing segment, with 
nearly 80% of Indian travellers now considering the 
accommodation experience central to their holiday — 
far above global averages. Short-break travel is rising, 
with 7-day-or-less itineraries becoming dominant. 
Drive-to destinations, heritage circuits, wildlife and 
wellness escapes are benefiting from improving road 
and rail connectivity.
Weddings and Social Events
The November–mid-December 2025 wedding window 
alone generated over ₹ 6.5 Lakh Crores (~$79 billion) across ~46 Lakh weddings — a ~10% growth over 
2024. Lemon Tree properties in leisure markets such 
as Jaipur, Goa and Udaipur are well-positioned to 
capitalise on this demand segment.
MICE
India’s infrastructure build-out for large-format 
events — Bharat Mandapam, Yashobhoomi, Jio World 
Convention Centre — is enabling events at a scale 
previously constrained by capacity. MICE demand is 
increasingly extending beyond the traditional top three 
metros, with Hyderabad, Jaipur and Kochi gaining 
significant convention credibility.
Airlines and Crew/Transit
The normalisation of aviation — despite IndiGo 
disruptions in Q3 FY 2025-26 — continues to generate 
consistent demand for airport-adjacent properties. 
India’s total air passenger traffic of 420 million in 
CY2025 and the rapid expansion of regional routes 
under UDAN support occupancy at airport properties 
and secondary cities.

Integrated Annual Report 2025-266. Key Risks and Mitigation Strategies
Seasonality Risk
•  Risk: Fluctuating occupancy and RevPAR across 
seasons, particularly in leisure-heavy markets
•  Mitigation: Diversified portfolio presence across 
80+ cities balances business and leisure demand 
cycles. Dynamic pricing engines and corporate 
contracts with semi-annual rate locks anchor base 
occupancy
Geopolitical and External Disruption Risk
•  Risk: Ongoing Middle East instability and 
aviation disruptions (as seen with IndiGo in Q3 
FY 2025- 26) create intermittent demand volatility
•  Mitigation:  India’s deep domestic demand base 
— over 4.5 billion domestic tourist visits — acts 
as a structural insulator against global shocks. 
Geopolitical disruptions in competing destinations 
such as the Middle East are expected to redirect 
international demand toward stable alternatives 
including India
5. Barriers to Entry  
Land Cost & Scarcity:  Land cost and 
scarcity in Tier I cities, which continue to 
constrain new supply in gateway markets
Regulatory Complexity:  Complex 
regulatory approvals, including 
environmental clearances, that extend 
project timelines
Capital Intensity:  High capital 
requirements with extended gestation 
periods and low ROI at sub-scale 
operations
Brand Entrenchment:  Brand loyalty 
and market saturation by established 
multi-brand operators in mature urban 
markets
Financing Constraints: Infrastructure 
lending thresholds (current ₹ 200 Crores 
qualifying limit) that restrict access to 
cheaper long-term capital for midscale 
projectsEconomic and Industry Risk
•  Risk: Rising crude oil prices (Brent crude above 
$111/barrel in parts of FY 2025-26) increase 
Aviation Turbine Fuel costs, driving airfare inflation 
that disproportionately impacts mid-market leisure 
travellers
•  Mitigation:  Multi-brand architecture spanning 
economy to upscale, combined with strong drive-
to destination positioning, provides a natural 
hedge against airfare sensitivity. Centralized 
procurement and supplier optimisation reduce 
exposure to input cost inflation
Financial Risk
•  Risk: Interest rate volatility, elevated working 
capital requirements and long project gestation 
periods
•  Mitigation:  Asset-light expansion through 
management contracts and franchise agreements 
limits balance sheet exposure while enabling 
rapid portfolio growth. Stable EBITDA margins 
and disciplined capital allocation support debt 
serviceability and investor confidence
T echnology and Competitive Risk
•  Risk: Algorithm-led travel discovery means hotels 
with weak digital presence risk losing bookings to 
better-optimised compe titors
•  Mitigation:  Investments in AI-driven revenue 
management, dynamic pricing infrastructure and 
OTA visibility are critical co untermeasures
7. Outlook for FY 2026-27 //CY2026
India’s hotel sector enters FY 2026-27/CY2026 from a position of structural strength, with industry-level RevPAR 
forecast for CY2026  to reach ~₹ 5,988 with occupancy at ~67% and ARR at ~₹ 8,931 — representing continued 
healthy growth over CY2025 levels.

The following macro-trends are expected to shape the operating environment for the industry:
Domestic T ourism as Structural Anchor
Domestic tourist visits are projected to cross 9,542 
million by 2030, based on a historical CAGR of 13.1% 
(2011–2019). Rising disposable incomes, improving 
multimodal connectivity and a broadening travel 
aspirations base — extending beyond the top metros 
into Tier II-IV markets — are the primary structural 
drivers.
Faith-Based and Event-Led T ourism
The Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj drew over 663 million 
visitors in 45 days , with an estimated economic 
impact exceeding ₹ 2 trillion. Live events are emerging 
as measurable demand generators: India hosted over 
34,000 live events in CY2025, with attendance growing 
17% year-on-year. The IPL drove occupancies above 
85% in host cities with F&B footfall up 40–50%.
Destination Weddings
India’s destination wedding segment — estimated at 
over $18 billion in CY2025  — is expanding at a 
steady double-digit pace. More than 60% of weddings 
with budgets exceeding ₹ 1 Crore are now destination-
based, with average spend climbing to ~₹ 58 Lakhs 
per wedding. This represents a high-yield, repeatable 
demand cycle that benefits midscale and upscale 
properties across leisure markets.MICE and the New Geography of Demand
MICE demand is decentralising rapidly. Cities like 
Hyderabad, Jaipur, Kochi and Indore are increasingly 
hosting large-format conferences and conventions, 
supported by purpose-built venues such as Bharat 
Mandapam and Yashobhoomi. Delegate expectations 
increasingly integrate leisure experiences into 
conference stays, benefiting Lemon Tree’s presence in 
emerging MICE cities.
AI-Driven Travel Planning
Over 83% of Indian travellers believe AI makes 
travel easier, with more than 80% using it to avoid 
overcrowding and discover experiences. India’s AI-in-
tourism market, valued at ~$109 million in CY2024, is 
projected to grow at a 32.6% CAGR to ~$595 million 
by 2030. For hospitality operators, this necessitates 
investment in digital visibility, structured content and 
dynamic pricing infrastructure to remain competitive in 
an algorithm-led discovery environment.
Tier 2–4 Market Expansion
Tier III and IV cities accounted for 44% of total hotel 
brand signings by keys in CY2025 and over 55% of 
properties signed.

as a core national priority, with a ₹ 2,438 Crores

For Lemon Tree Hotels, the convergence of a maturing 
rate-led cycle, deepening Tier II-IV penetration, 
growing MICE and wedding demand in secondary 
cities and the rising importance of the accommodation 
experience as a travel anchor all represent compelling 
structural tailwinds. The Company’s diversified brand 
architecture, disciplined asset-light expansion strategy 
and entrenched domestic demand focus position it well 
to deliver sustained RevPAR improvement and margin 
expansion through FY 2026-27/CY2026 and beyond.

The Company’s total income has increased by 13% 
from ` 1,288.4 Crores during FY 2024-25 to ` 1,452.7 
Crores during FY 2025-26 and revenue from operations 
alone increased by 12% from ` 1,286.1 Crores for  
FY 2024-25 to ` 1,444.5 Crores for FY 2025-26.
•  Gross ARR of the Company saw an increase of 8% 
from ` 6,381 in FY 2024-25 to ` 6,875 in FY 2025-26; 
Occupancy increased by 186 bps from 71.7% in  
FY 2024-25 to 73.5% in FY 2025-26; hence, the 
RevPAR increased by 11% from ` 4,573 in  
FY 2024-25 to ` 5,055 in FY 2025-26
•  The revenue from food and beverages increased 
by 10% from ` 247.5 Crores for FY 2024-25 to  
` 271.6 Crores for FY 2025-26
•  The management fees from third-party owned 
hotels also increased by 23% from ` 60.3 Crores 
for FY 2024-25 to ` 73.9 Crores for FY 2025-26
Expenses
Total expenses increased by 16% from ` 652.0 Crores 
for FY 2024-25 to ` 753.3 Crores for FY 2025-26.
•  The cost of food and beverages consumed 
increased in line with the increase in food and 
beverages revenue from ` 76.2 Crores for  
FY 2024- 25 to ` 84.8 Crores for FY 2025-26.  
Moreover, the cost of food and beverages 
consumed as a percentage of food and beverages 
revenue has increased from 30.8% for FY 2024-25 
to 31.2% for FY 2025-26
•  Employee Benefit expenses increased by 10% 
from ` 218.5 Crores for  FY 2024-25 to ` 239.3 
Crores for FY 2025-26 primarily due to a one-time 
ex-gratia payment made to hotel employees as 
a goodwill gesture linked to salary rationalization 
measures implemented during the COVID-19 
period
•  Power and Fuel expenses decreased by 3% from  
` 87.8 Crores for FY 2024-25 to ` 85.1 Crores for  
FY 2025-26 driven by increased adoption of 
renewable energy sources
•  Other expenses increased by 28% from ` 269.5 
Crores for FY 2024-25 to ` 344.2 Crores for  
FY 2025- 26 driven by higher business activity, the 
impact of changes in GST regulations resulting 
in lower input tax credit benefits and increased 
renovation expenditure across the portfolioNet EBITDA
The Company’s net EBITDA increased by 10% from  
` 636.5 Crores for FY 2024-25 to ` 699.3 Crores for  
FY 2025- 26. Net EBITDA margins decreased by 126 bps 
from 49.4% for FY 2024-25 to 48.1% for FY 2025-26, 
largely on account of reduced GST input tax credit benefits 
following regulatory changes and increased renovation-
related expenditure across the portfolio.
Depreciation and Amortization
Depreciation and amortization expenses remained 
almost flat, at ` 139.3 Crores for FY 2024-25 and 
slightly came down to ` 138.8 Crores for FY 2025-26.
Finance Costs
Total debt decreased by 12% from ` 1,698.6 Crores for  
FY 2024-25 to ` 1,500.3 Crores for FY 2025-26. The 
finance cost decreased by 15% from ` 211.2 Crores for  
FY 2024-25 to ` 179.5 Crores for FY 2025-26. The 
Company’s weighted average cost of debt decreased 
by 115 bps from 8.57% as at end of FY 2024-25 to 
7.42% as at end of FY 2025-26.
Exceptional Items

•  Considering uniform definition of ‘wages’ as

` 14.5 Crores

paid to certain employees as a goodwill gesture 
in connection with salary rationalization measures 
undertaken during the COVID-19 period
•  The Company availed a one-time settlement 
scheme notified by the Municipal Corporation of 
Delhi for settlement of property tax dues relating 
to three hotel properties resulting to an impact

•  The Company spent ` 3.0 Crores towards

2026, subject to requisite statutory and regulatory 
approvals

STATEMENT OF COMPANY’S AFFAIRS:
A.  Operational Hotels and Upcoming Projects
  During the year under review, the Company 
achieved the significant milestone of crossing 
11,000 operational rooms. As on March 31, 2026, 
the Group’s portfolio comprised 131 operational 
hotels with 11,811 rooms, while the development 
pipeline consisted of 137 hotels with 10,770 rooms.
  Lemon Tree Hotels Limited is a Company engaged 
in hotel business and there has been no change in 
the nature of its business during the year under 
review.

The Company has, in place, Risk Management Policy

that the applicable risks need to be managed and 
mitigated to protect the interests of the shareholders and

sustainable growth. The risk management framework is 
aimed at effectively mitigating the Company’s various 
business and operational risks, through strategic and 
tactical actions. Risk management is embedded in our 
critical business activities, functions and processes. 
The risks are reviewed for the change in the nature 
and extent of the major risks which provides control 
measures for risks and future action plans.

PARTICULARS REGARDING CONSERVATION 
OF ENERGY ETC. UNDER SECTION 134(3)(m) 
OF THE COMPANIES ACT, 2013 AND RULES 
MADE THEREIN
As per the provisions of Section 134(3)(m) of the Act 
read with Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2013, the 
measures taken during the Financial Year under review 
for conservation of energy and technology absorption 
by the Company in the operation of its hotels are as 
follows:
A.  Conservation of Energy:
  Lemon Tree Hotels is deeply committed to 
ecofriendly operations and energy conservation 
=== page 94 ===
156Lemon Tree Hotels Limited
Integrated Annual Report 2025-26practices across all its properties. We believe 
that sustainability is integral to hospitality, and 
accordingly, we have implemented a wide range of 
initiatives focused on energy and water preservation, 
responsible waste management, and measures to 
mitigate water, noise, and environmental pollution.
  Our existing and upcoming owned hotels are 
designed and constructed in line with IGBC Green 
Building Certification Standards, ensuring that 
sustainability is embedded right from the planning 
and design stage. These efforts reflect our longterm 
vision of reducing environmental impact while 
enhancing operational efficiency.
  Further, the detailed steps undertaken for energy 
conservation and sustainability are comprehensively 
documented in the Business Responsibility and 
Sustainability Report (BRSR), which forms an 
integral part of this Report.
  Steps taken by the Company for utilizing 
alternate source of energy:
  The Company has consistently prioritized the use 
of alternative and renewable sources of energy to 
enhance sustainability across its operations. Our 
hotels have installed onsite Solar Photovoltaic 
(PV) systems on rooftops, enabling clean 
electricity generation and reducing dependence 
on conventional grid supply. In addition, solar hot 
water systems have been deployed to significantly 
lower the heating load for domestic hot water 
requirements, thereby improving energy efficiency.
  Beyond onsite installations, we are also 
leveraging renewable energy through Open 
Access arrangements, which currently cater 
to approximately 50% of our total energy 
requirement. This integrated approach-combining 
rooftop solar generation, solar thermal systems, 
and Open Access procurement-demonstrates 
our commitment to reducing carbon footprint, 
optimizing operational costs, and aligning with 
longterm sustainability goals.  The Capital investment on energy conservation 
requirements:
  The Company has made significant capital 
investments in sustainable technologies to 
reduce reliance on fossil fuels and enhance 
energy efficiency across its hotels. Rooftop Solar 
Photovoltaic (PV) systems have been installed to 
generate clean electricity onsite, directly lowering 
grid dependency. To minimize diesel consumption, 
heat pumps are being used in place of conventional 
hot water generators, providing efficient heating 
solutions. Additionally, heat recovery systems 
have been implemented to improve ventilation 
efficiency, while EC fan motors are deployed in 
HVAC and ventilation systems to optimize energy 
use.
  Further, the adoption of double-glazed windows in 
guest rooms and public areas enhances thermal 
insulation, reduces cooling and heating loads, 
and improves overall comfort. Collectively, these 
measures not only reduce operational costs but 
also demonstrate the Company’s commitment 
to sustainability, energy conservation, and 
environmental responsibility.
B.   Technology Absorption, Research & 
Development (R&D):
 Technology absorption:
  The Company is in the service industry and 
operates and manages its hotels across India. 
However, no know how and technology has been 
imported during the year. However, efforts have 
been made to imbibe various new technologies 
like Green Building, rain water harvesting, use of 
plumbing faucets, sewage treatment plants.
 Research & Development:
  The Company operates in the hospitality sector 
where formal Research and Development (‘R&D’) 
investments are limited. During the year under 
review no expenditure was incurred for R&D 
purposes.

1. Introduction
  In terms of Section 178 of the Companies Act, 
2013 read with applicable rules and regulations 
and in pursuance of the policy of Lemon Tree 
Hotels Limited (‘Company’) to consider its human 
resources as its invaluable assets, the Nomination 
and Remuneration Committee of the Company re-
constituted on 18th September 2014 has formulated 
this policy on nomination and remuneration of 
Directors, Key managerial personnel, senior 
management personnel and other employees of 
the Company (hereinafter referred as ‘Policy’) and 
which has been adopted by Board of Directors of 
the Company in its meeting on February 19th, 2015.
 Policy Objective
  The objective of this Policy is to determine the 
criteria for appointment, removal, evaluation 
of performance of Directors and remuneration 
of Directors, key managerial personnel, senior 
management personnel and other employees.
2.	 Definitions
 In this Policy unless the context otherwise requires:
 (a)  “Act” means Companies Act, 2013 including 
the applicable Rules & regulations;
 (b)  “Board of Directors” or “Board”, in relation to 
the Company, means the collective body of 
the directors of the Company and includes the 
committees of the Board;
 (c)  “Directors” means Directors of the Company 
appointed in terms of provisions of the Act;
 (d)  “Independent Director” means a Director 
referred to in Section 149 (6) of the Act;
 (e)  “Key Managerial Personnel ”or“KMP” in relation 
to a company, means:
  (i)   Chief Executive Officer (‘CEO’) or the 
Managing Director (‘MD’) or the Manager;
  (ii) Company Secretary;
  (iii) Whole-time Director (‘WTD’);
  (iv) Chief Financial Officer; and
  (v) Such other officer as may be prescribed;
 (f)  “NRC” means Nomination and Remuneration 
Committee of the Company as constituted or 
reconstituted by the Board; (g)  “Rules & regulations” refers to and comprise 
of Companies Act, 2013, The Companies 
(Meeting of Board and its Powers) Rules, 
2014, The Companies (Appointment and 
Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014, The 
Companies (Appointment and Remuneration 
of Managerial personnel) Rules, 2014, and 
such other rules and provisions as applicable 
to the matters dealt in by this Policy;
 (h)  *”Senior Management Personnel” for this 
purpose shall mean employees of the company 
who are members of its core management 
team excluding Board of Directors including 
CFO and CS. It would comprise of all members 
of management at Band level 12 & above who 
are designated at Executive Vice President/ 
President/ Senior Vice President and are 
directly reporting to Executive Chairman or 
Managing Director along with employees of the 
Company/Group who have been specifically 
designated as Senior Management due to their 
role and responsibilities.
  Unless the context otherwise requires, words 
and expressions used in this policy and not 
defined herein but defined in the Act as may be 
amended from time to time shall have the meaning 
respectively assigned to them therein.
  *Definition of Senior Management Personnel amended 
w.e.f. April 1, 2024
3. Applicability
 This Policy is applicable to:
 (i)  Directors viz. Executive, Non-executive and 
Independent
 (ii) Key Managerial Personnel
 (iii) Senior Management Personnel
 (iv) Other Employees of the Company
4. General
 This Policy is divided in three parts:
  Part-A: covers the matters to be dealt with and 
recommended by the NRC to the Board within 
Scope of Policy;
  Part-B: covers the appointment and nomination of 
Directors; and
  Part-C: covers remuneration etc. for the Directors, 
Key Managerial Personnel and other employees.‘Annexure-2’
Nomination and Remuneration Policy
